name: Hilot

card.summary: Hilot is Filipino traditional massage and bone-setting, used by practitioners and clients for muscle and joint comfort, postpartum recovery and relaxation that can support posture, movement and a rested look.
card.note: Techniques vary by practitioner; forceful joint manipulation by untrained practitioners has been raised as a concern.

quick.overview:
Hilot is the traditional healing art of the Philippines, centered on massage and hands-on manipulation of muscles, tendons and joints. Practitioners, called manghihilot, are consulted for sprains, aches, stiffness and recovery after childbirth.

For appearance, the appeal runs through comfort and recovery: looser muscles and easier movement can support better posture and a more relaxed, rested look. Published descriptions treat it mainly as a cultural practice, and trials of its techniques have not been published.
quick.how: A session is typically a hands-on massage, sometimes with oils or herbal preparations, and may include joint resetting for sprains, suction cupping (bentosa) or prayer and ritual elements, depending on the practitioner. It is often used alongside everyday care for aches and after childbirth.
quick.risks: Gentle massage is generally low risk, but forceful manipulation of joints or bones by an untrained practitioner can aggravate an injury, and skilled-practitioner quality varies. People with fractures, pregnancy complications or other medical conditions are usually advised by clinicians to have them assessed in a medical setting first.

lead: Hilot is a traditional Filipino healing practice built around massage and manual manipulation. Its practitioners, known as manghihilot, work on muscles, tendons and joints, and are traditionally consulted for sprains, dislocations, chronic aches and care after childbirth. Techniques vary between practitioners, and some add herbs, prayer or ritual.

In looks-improvement terms, hilot is a body-comfort practice: people use it for tension relief and easier movement, which feeds into posture, how they carry themselves and a rested appearance. Related practitioners include albularyo (herbalists) and magpapaanak (traditional midwives).

The Traditional and Alternative Medicine Act of 1997 sought to bring traditional practices into Philippine healthcare, and a government institute promotes their continuation. Hilot-related literature in biomedical journals is mostly about traditional birth attendants, also called hilots, and their role in rural maternal health and family planning; trials of the massage techniques themselves are not available.

chain: Better posture and a more relaxed, rested look
angle.text: People use hilot for muscle tension, sprains and postpartum recovery. Easier movement and less tightness can feed into posture and general presentation. It is a recovery and comfort practice rather than a direct appearance treatment.

infobox: Philippines; described as pre-colonial in origin [1]

paras: The word hilot is associated in Tagalog with rubbing and soothing strokes [1]. Manghihilot apply massage and manual pressure to muscles, joints and nerves and are asked to treat sprains, strains and postpartum recovery [1]. Wikipedia describes bio-mechanical work resembling chiropractic, herbal preparations from albularyo practitioners, and spiritual forms such as the Banahaw devotional technique, tied to prayer and rituals at Mount Banahaw.

Practitioners describe health as balance (timbang) among bodily humors, energies and the environment [1]. Related techniques mentioned in descriptions include pulse reading, acupressure-like pressure points and suction cupping known as bentosa [1].
Accounts trace hilot to pre-colonial healing and shamanic traditions of the archipelago, transmitted orally across generations [1]. Wikipedia notes that this origin is not well sourced.

Government attitudes shifted over time. A 1977 report says the state discouraged hilot practice until the early 1950s, then permitted it; in 1955 the Department of Health and the WHO began a training program for traditional birth attendants called hilots [2]. A 1970s survey identified more than 31,000 practicing hilots, who attended roughly 40 to 48 percent of registered births in the early 1970s [2][3]. The Traditional and Alternative Medicine Act of 1997 aimed to integrate traditional practice into rural healthcare, and the Philippine Institute of Traditional and Alternative Health Care promotes hilot. Wikipedia notes that stigma and limited scholarly evidence keep it contested in public health policy.

Proponents describe hilot as effective for sprains and pain based on generations of practice [1]. Commentary summarized by Grokipedia states that its efficacy remains largely anecdotal and that risks arise from unqualified practitioners who might worsen injuries through improper manipulation [1]. Claims about adjusting energy frequencies have not been tested in controlled trials [1].

No studies found on hilot massage as a technique. Published research on hilots concerns traditional birth attendants: surveys of their numbers and training programs and their role in family-planning outreach in the Philippines [2][3].

timeline.event: Philippine Department of Health and WHO begin training hilots as birth attendants [2].
National survey identifies about 31,200 practicing hilots [3].
Traditional and Alternative Medicine Act passed to integrate traditional medicine.
